title: The Scandal at 1612 Prairie
premise: A carriage maker's fancy house has become the most talked-about house on the block. There is a divorce, a judge's order, a violin in a broken car, and a small boy caught in the middle.

opening.text:
JAUNT: THE SCANDAL AT 1612 PRAIRIE. It is a Monday afternoon in November 1904, at the quiet north end of Prairie Avenue.

There are four stops along one short block. For twenty years the house at 1612 was one of the finest on the street. This year it is the scene of a big fight. A husband and wife are getting a divorce. A judge has let the wife keep the house. In November the husband stood up in court and said things about her that the whole city has now read in the newspaper. The neighbors keep their curtains closed and their ears open.

Start next door, where you can picture the house the way it used to be.

stops.text: This is 1608 Prairie, and next to it is the big square house at 1612. Twenty years ago it belonged to a Studebaker. The Studebaker brothers made carriages. Theirs was the brightest house on the street. In 1884 about two hundred guests came here after a family wedding. Every room was lit up and filled with flowers and green vines. A newspaper said that morning and night, a fancy carriage stood in front of the door. A carriage maker's house should have the best carriages, and it did. Look at it now. No carriage waits at the curb today. A maid next door is watching from her steps. Walk to the gate of 1612.

stage.caption: A maid at 1608 sweeps her steps and keeps one eye on the house next door.

stops.text: This is 1612 Prairie. The newspaper has the story, and so does everybody else. Last May the husband, Charles Brown, asked a court for a divorce. His wife, Catherine, is 27. She is the daughter of a rich general from Buffalo. Mr. Brown said she drank too much and did other wrong things. Then a judge, Judge Tuley, let Mrs. Brown keep living in this house. He also ordered Mr. Brown to pay her $200 a month until the case was over. So the wife is inside, and the husband is outside. Behind those windows live a woman the papers have made famous and a small boy. The house will be torn down around 1960. Step next door to hear what the husband said in November.

stage.caption: A lady comes out on the steps of 1612. She looks up and down the street and goes back in quickly.

cast.name: Catherine G. Brown (no card in the town; an unnamed figure plays her)

stops.text: This is 1616 Prairie, the house next door to the south. The neighbors here read the newspaper with their breakfast. In November Mr. Brown went back to court. He said his wife often drank too much and did very strange things. He said she once played a violin in a broken car while a man pushed it down the road. He said she danced behind the house in her nightgown. He also said she had run away with another man, a car salesman, first to a summer town and then to New York. It is the juiciest gossip on Prairie Avenue in years, and two maids on these steps are enjoying it. But a divorce is not only about two people. Look for the boy.

stage.caption: Two maids on the steps of 1616 share the newspaper and look over at 1612.

stops.text: Cross to 1613 and look back at the other side of the block. The boy is Charles Edward Brown, the couple's only son. He is the real prize in this fight. A nurse walks him along the sidewalk past his own front door. His mother has the house. His father wants the house back, and he wants the boy too. The court has not decided yet. In the newspapers the boy is just one line at the end of each story. On this walk he is the only person in the whole fight who has done nothing wrong at all. The story will end in March 1905.

stage.caption: A nurse walks a small boy along the far sidewalk past the door of 1612. He stops to look up at it.

cast.name: Charles Edward Brown, the son (no card in the town; an unnamed figure plays him)
A nurse of the Brown household (unnamed)

legs.story: A few steps south to the gate of 1612, the house the whole street is watching.
Next door south, to the neighbors with the morning newspaper.
Across Prairie Avenue to look back at the other side of the block.

endings.text: The walk ends here. Early in 1905, after a hard fight, the husband won. He got the divorce, the house and the boy. On 8 March 1905 he sold the house to the bishop of a Chicago church. That same week the newspaper found Catherine Brown in jail. The police had arrested her at another house, where they said she was using a different name. She had to pay a fine, but she said, "I am penniless," and, "I cannot pay the fine". The general's daughter from Buffalo had kept 1612 Prairie for less than a year.

keepsake.title: The 1612 Court Papers
keepsake.text: A card about the Brown divorce of 1904 and 1905, as the newspaper told it. It is a made-up keepsake, not an object from history.

evidence.text: On 21 February 1884 about 200 of the intimate friends and relatives of the bride and groom were received at the residence of W. F. Studebaker, No. 1612 Prairie avenue, after the Studebaker-Innis wedding. 'The large residence was brilliantly illuminated, and every room was elaborately decorated with smilax and cut flowers.'
evidence.locator: Chicago Tribune, 22 February 1884, 'Wedding Bells', as transcribed.

evidence.text: Inter Ocean, 2 January 1887: 'Morning and night, a showy turnout is noticed before the squarely-built house, with the number 1612 over the portals.' Its owner was one of the Studebaker Brothers, the carriage makers.

The Scandal at 1612 Prairie: the day, Monday 21 November 1904, the hour and the order of the walk are this jaunt's framing, chosen because the stories meet on it (three days after Arthur Caton's death, a Monday of the Reading Class, before Kimball's death in December). No visit on that day is asserted.

The Scandal at 1612 Prairie: who is seen at each stop, where they stand, what they do and when are reconstructed. People with cards in the town play themselves; people the town has no card for (and the unnamed servants, callers and passers-by) are unnamed figures in period dress, and no likeness is claimed. No word anyone says is asserted.

Catherine G. Brown was the 'former wife of Charles E. Brown, 1612 Prairie avenue'. Mrs. Brown, who is 27 years old and the daughter of Gen. Graves, a wealthy resident of Buffalo, first attracted notoriety in May, 1904, when her husband filed a bill for divorce. By a court order issued by Judge Tuley Mrs. Brown was given possession of the residence, 1612 Prairie avenue, where she and her husband and their son had lived, and was granted temporary alimony amounting to $200 a month while the suit was pending. Habitual drunkenness and statutory charges were the grounds.
evidence.locator: Chicago Tribune, 11 March 1905, 'Story of Divorce Case', as transcribed.

evidence.text: Joseph Goodman Residence, 1612 S. Prairie Avenue: razed circa 1960.

In November Mr. Brown appeared in court and charged that his wife had conducted herself in a disgraceful manner, had been habitually intoxicated, and had done many freakish things, such as playing a violin in a broken automobile while a man pushed the machine along a public highway, and dancing about the rear of their home clothed only in a nightrobe.
evidence.locator: Chicago Tribune, 11 March 1905, 'Story of Divorce Case', as transcribed.

evidence.text: He also charged her with receiving the attentions of E. C. Edsall, an automobile salesman. With Edsall, the husband charged, Mrs. Brown ran away to an eastern summer resort and later to New York City.
After a bitter fight Mr. Brown was granted a divorce about six weeks before 11 March 1905, and given possession of the Prairie avenue property, and the custody of the one son, Charles Edward Brown.
evidence.locator: Chicago Tribune, 11 March 1905, the last paragraph, as transcribed.

evidence.text: In March 1905 Mrs. Catherine G. Brown was arrested at 3667 Wabash avenue, where she had been living under the name of Kittie Casey, according to the police, and fined $85 for disorderly conduct. 'I am penniless,' she said. 'I cannot pay the fine.' In her cell she said: 'It's all because a woman is jealous of me, I guess.' Justice Hurley called her 'a problem in humanity to me.'
On 8 March 1905 the lot at 1612 Prairie passed from Brown (printed 'Chas. S. Brown') to the Rt. Rev. Chas. Palmerston Anderson, bishop of the Protestant Episcopal church in the diocese of Chicago.
evidence.locator: Chicago Tribune, 14 March 1905, the transfer list, as transcribed.
